opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the two are really two views of the same underlying problem: memory. When we talk about long-context understanding, we're usually asking how a model can keep using information it saw a while ago in the same sequence. Continual learning asks how a model keeps using what it saw a while ago across tasks or over its whole lifetime. The difference is mostly the timescale and where we choose to draw the boundary.

In a standard Transformer that boundary is very sharp. You have the weights, which are learned during pre-training and then frozen, and that's your long-term memory. Then you have the attention over the context window, which is a very precise short-term memory, but it's bounded and it vanishes once the context is gone. Nothing in between moves information from the short-term memory into the long-term one. That's why these models struggle with both problems. Past a certain length the context becomes too expensive or too diluted to use well, and anything the model learns at test time is simply lost.

The way I like to think about it, inspired a lot by how human memory works, is that we need a spectrum of memory systems that update at different frequencies. Some components should adapt very fast, token by token. Others should consolidate more slowly. And the slowest should hold stable knowledge. That's the motivation behind work like Titans and, more recently, nested learning. You treat parts of the model as memory modules that keep learning at test time. For example, they can update their parameters based on how "surprising" a new input is, with mechanisms for forgetting so the memory doesn't saturate.

Once you have that, long context stops being about how many tokens you can attend to at once. It becomes a question of how well the model can compress and store what matters. And continual learning stops being a separate training procedure you bolt on. It becomes the natural behavior of a system whose memory is always updating at multiple timescales. So from my perspective, if we really solve long-context understanding in the right way, by building models that learn to memorize at test time, we've made a big step toward continual learning too. The two problems converge.

r001.rationale: The response says long contexts can become costly or diluted, but does not state that increasing context-window size has improved performance across a broad range of evaluation tasks.

r002.rationale: It presents continual learning and long-context understanding as two views of the same memory problem, without characterizing continual learning as the more general capability.

r003.rationale: It says solving long-context understanding would advance continual learning, but does not express the reverse expectation that a successful continual learner would improve long-context understanding.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I actually think these two problems are much closer than people usually treat them, and in some sense they're almost the same problem viewed from two angles.

When we talk about long-context understanding, we're asking: can the model take in a huge stream of information and, at the end, use the relevant pieces of it? When we talk about continual learning, we're asking: can the model keep updating itself on new data without forgetting what it already knows? In both cases the core challenge is memory. You have information arriving over time, you can't keep all of it in raw form, and you have to decide what to store, how to store it, and how to retrieve it later.

The way I like to think about it is that a Transformer's attention is essentially a memory that doesn't compress. It stores every token exactly, and that's why it's so accurate in-context, but it's also why it becomes expensive and why it hits a wall at some fixed window. Recurrent models and linear attention go the other way: they compress everything into a fixed-size state, which is cheap, but a fixed-size state can only hold so much, and it tends to overwrite old information when new information comes in. That overwriting is literally catastrophic forgetting, just happening at the level of a single forward pass instead of across training runs.

So in our work, things like Titans and the follow-up directions, the idea is to treat the model's memory as something that learns at test time. Instead of a fixed update rule, you have a memory module whose parameters get updated with gradient-like steps as tokens arrive, with a notion of surprise deciding what's worth writing, and a forgetting mechanism deciding what can be released. Once you frame it that way, long context becomes online learning: processing a very long sequence is the same as continually learning from a stream. And continual learning across tasks becomes a question of how to design the memory so that writing new things doesn't destroy old things, which is exactly the capacity and interference problem you face with long sequences.

The other piece I'd emphasize is that this is about more than architecture. The optimizer matters too, because if your memory updates with something like momentum or a learned step size, the quality of what you remember depends heavily on how those updates are shaped. That's part of why we've been pushing on viewing architectures and optimization together as different layers of a nested system, where each level is learning and remembering at its own timescale.

So to answer directly: long-context understanding is continual learning within a sequence, and continual learning is long-context understanding across a lifetime. If you can build a memory system that handles one well, with the right balance of plasticity and stability, you're most of the way to handling the other.

r001.rationale: The response discusses context-window costs and memory, but does not say that increasing the context window has been observed to improve performance across a broad range of evaluation tasks.

r002.rationale: It describes continual learning and long-context understanding as closely related or nearly the same problem, not continual learning as the more general capability.

r003.rationale: It says that if a memory system handles either problem well, it is most of the way to handling the other, and frames long-context understanding as continual learning within a sequence. This conveys that successful continual learning is expected to improve long-context understanding.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re closely related because both are about how a model incorporates new information. With long context, you give the model information at inference time, and it can use that information without necessarily changing its parameters. With continual learning, you’re asking how the model can keep learning from a stream of experience and retain what matters over time.

The connection becomes clearer when you think of context as a form of memory. Attention gives you a way to retrieve information from that memory. Learning gives you a way to compress information into a persistent state. Those have different tradeoffs: keeping the context lets you revisit details, while compressing it can be more efficient, but you have to decide what to preserve.

So I wouldn’t say that a longer context window automatically solves continual learning. Being able to access something is different from learning from it. But I do think the two problems point toward a shared question: how should a model update and use its memory as new information arrives, without losing the knowledge it still needs?

r001.rationale: The response explains that long context provides information at inference time, but does not say that increasing the context window has been observed to improve performance across evaluation tasks.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes continual learning from long-context understanding and describes their tradeoffs, but does not characterize continual learning as the more general capability.

r003.rationale: It calls the problems closely related, but does not express an expectation that successful continual learning would improve long-context understanding.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re very closely related. In both cases, the model receives information over time and needs to retain what matters so it can use it later. In long-context understanding, we usually put that information in the context window. In continual learning, we usually think about incorporating it into the model’s parameters. But both raise the same question: how do you update your memory without losing useful information you already have?

The distinction is partly about the timescale and the mechanism of adaptation. Attention gives you a way to access information in the current context, while learning gives you a way to compress information into a persistent state. And there’s a spectrum between those two: you can have a memory that updates as the model processes a sequence, rather than keeping the weights completely fixed during inference.

From that perspective, a long context is not just a storage problem. Making more tokens available doesn’t necessarily mean the model can learn from them or use them effectively. You need a mechanism for deciding what to remember, what to update, and what to forget. Those are also central problems in continual learning. So I see them as two views of a broader problem: how a system adapts to a stream of information.

r002.rationale: It presents continual learning and long-context understanding as closely related views of a broader problem, without saying continual learning is the more general capability.

r003.rationale: It does not express an expectation that successful continual learning would improve long-context understanding.
